item.title: Data Challenge - Image recovery
item.dc:creator: Athos Damiani
Daniel Falbel
Bruna Wundervald
item.description:
Files with the .jpg extension store 5 coordinates, which are enough for the computer to understand and draw the image:

  • x and y: the cartesian coordinates of the image; and
  • r, g and b: red, green and blue, respectively, which together form colors.

Every color we know can be made by combining these three colors. The intensity of each color ranges from 0 to 1. For each point on the (x,y) plane there is an associated color. So an image can be represented by a dataset with 5 columns (x, y, r, g and b) whose number of rows is the number of pixels in the image.

Goals

  • Find out which model, linear regression or decision trees, is the most suitable to recover the blue component of the purple_wave.jpg image.

  • Find out which model, linear regression or decision trees, is the most suitable to recover the blue component of the xadrez_colorido.jpg image.

How to start?

With the help of the readJPEG() function from the jpeg package, load one of the images into R and turn it into a data.frame:

library(tidyverse)
library(jpeg)
# loads a jpeg image into R
download.file("http://curso-r.comimages/posts/conteudo/desafio-recuperacao-img/purple_wave.webp", 
              destfile = "purple_wave.jpg")

img <- readJPEG("purple_wave.jpg")

# turns the image array into a data.frame with position (x,y)
# and color (r,g,b) info; image dimensions
img_dim <- dim(img)

# RGB to data.frame
img_df <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:img_dim[2], each = img_dim[1]),
  y = rep(img_dim[1]:1, img_dim[2]),
  r = as.vector(img[,,1]),
  g = as.vector(img[,,2]),
  b = as.vector(img[,,3])
) %>%
  mutate(cor = rgb(r, g, b),
         id = 1:n())

Split the data.frame into two parts: one with the blue (column b) and one without. - Part 1) x, y, r, g - Part 2) x, y, r, g, b

# for reproducibility
set.seed(2018) 
# Part 1) x, y, r, g
img_df_parte1 <- img_df %>% 
  sample_frac(3/5) %>% # taking 3/5 of the dataset
  mutate(b_backup = b, # backup of the original blue
         b = 0, # removing the blue from the image
         cor = rgb(r, g, b)) # image color without the blue
# Part 2) x, y, r, g, b
img_df_parte2 <- img_df %>% filter(!id%in%img_df_parte1$id)

Visualizing:

# Image without the blue
ggplot(data = img_df_parte1, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point(colour = img_df_parte1$cor) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", title = "Imagem sem B (azul)") +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  theme_bw()

Your task is to recover the blue (which we erased from the image) in Part 1, using predictive models built with Part 2 (which still has the blue!) for both images (xadrez_colorido and purple_wave).

Result

The result of this data challenge will be published on the blog on August 24! Good luck!

item.title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
item.dc:creator: Athos Damiani
Julio Trecenti
item.description:
Tree-based models like decision trees, random forest, ligthGBM and xgboost are known, among other qualities, for their robustness to multicollinearity. It’s well known that their predictive power isn’t shaken by the presence of extremely correlated variables.

But who has never used a Random Forest for variable selection? Taking, for example, the top 10 most important ones and dropping the rest?

Or even ventured an interpretation and drew conclusions from the order of the most important variables?

Below we show why we shouldn’t ignore multicollinearity completely!

A nice little model

First let’s fit a nice little model, free of multicollinearity. Suppose we want to predict Petal.Length using the sepal measurements (Sepal.Width and Sepal.Length) from our good old iris dataset.

library(tidyverse)

iris2 <- iris %>% select(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length)
iris2 %>% cor %>% corrplot::corrplot()

The plot above shows that the explanatory variables are not strongly correlated. Fitting a random fores, we get the following variable importance order:

library(randomForest)
iris2_rf <- randomForest(Petal.Length ~ ., data = iris2)
varImpPlot(iris2_rf)

No surprises. Now on to the problem!

An ugly model

Let’s forge an extreme situation where many variables are multicollinear. I’ll do this by repeating the Sepal.Length column several times.

iris3 <- accumulate(1:20, ~{
  .x[[paste0("Sepal.Length", .y)]] <-  iris2$Sepal.Length
  .x
}, .init = iris2)

iris3[[20]] %>% cor %>% corrplot::corrplot(order = "alphabet")

Now things are ugly! We have 20 perfectly collinear variables. Even so, a random forest on this new dataset wouldn’t lose predictive power.

But what happened to the variable importance?

iris3_rf <- randomForest(Petal.Length ~ ., data = iris3[[20]])
varImpPlot(iris3_rf)

Here the tables have turned: we would conclude that Sepal.Width is the most important of all the variables!

Flawed variable selection

The plot below shows that the more correlated variables we have, the lower the importance of ALL OF THEM AT THE SAME TIME! It’s as if the collinear variables split the importance among themselves.

# fits a random forest on datasets with 1 to 20 repetitions of `Sepal.Length`
rfs <- map(iris3, ~ randomForest(Petal.Length ~ ., data = .x) %>% importance)

# extracts the importances of the `Sepal.Length` repetitions
importancia <- map_dfr(rfs, ~{
  .x %>% 
    as.data.frame() %>% 
    tibble::rownames_to_column() %>% 
    dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(rowname, "^Sepal.Length"))
}, .id = "n_repeticoes") %>%
  mutate(n_repeticoes = as.numeric(n_repeticoes))

# Plot of the number of multicollinear variables vs importance
importancia %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_repeticoes, y = IncNodePurity)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 40, size = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Qtd de repetições da coluna `Sepal.Length`", y = "Importância", title = "Gráfico da relação entre o número de variáveis multicolineares vs importância")

In practice, if we set an importance cutoff to drop variables (as illustrated by the red line), we would have a potential problem: we could be throwing away very important information.

So how do we deal with multicollinearity?

Some ways to deal with multicollinearity are:

  • Looking at the correlation matrix
  • VIF
  • Recursive feature elimination

Conclusion

Be careful when throwing everything into the pot! We should always worry about multicollinearity, even when fitting tree-based models.

Cheers!

item.title: Bring it on - Guess The Correlation Kaggle Competition
item.dc:creator: Athos Damiani
item.description:
Hellooo community

We launched a Kaggle competition and now it’s time to show you are a DATA SCIENCE Jedi! =D

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/c/guess-the-correlation/

We did this for sport, please don’t try to find any use for this application =P.

The Game

The Guess The Correlation website puts a human face to face with a scatterplot and then challenges them to guess its linear correlation.

Our Kaggle challenge is built the same way. For example: what would you guess is the correlation of the data in the figure below?

We generated 200 thousand png images like the one above, and each one has its correlation labeled so we can train a little model.

Goal

The goal is simple and direct: build a robot that computes the (linear) correlation just by looking at the scatterplot.

In machine learnese, we want

where this f is worthy of being the f in F@!#.

Initial guess

Julião has already been working on this problem and took an initial shot at the code for you to get inspired. Well, “initial” is a stretch, because he went straight to a CNN with the help of the decryptr package:

library(keras)
library(tidyverse)
library(decryptr)

path <- "."
arqs <- dir(paste0(path,  "/train_imgs"), full.names = TRUE)
resp <- readr::read_csv(paste0(path,  "/train_responses.csv"))

i_train <- sample(1:nrow(resp), 10000)
arqs_train <- arqs[i_train]
arqs_test <- arqs[-i_train]

gen <- function(batch_size = 100, arqs = arqs_train) {
  f <- function() {
    a <- sort(sample(arqs, batch_size))
    imgs <- decryptr::read_captcha(a)
    captchas_t <- purrr::transpose(imgs)
    xs <- captchas_t$x
    xs <- abind::abind(xs, along = 0.1)
    a_clean <- a %>% 
      basename() %>% 
      tools::file_path_sans_ext() %>% 
      tolower()
    corr <- resp %>% 
      filter(id %in% a_clean) %>% 
      arrange(id) %>% 
      pull(corr)
    data <- list(xs, corr)
    data
  }
  f
}


# Create model
model <- keras_model_sequential()
model %>%
  layer_conv_2d(
    input_shape = c(150, 150, 1),
    filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
    padding = "same",
    activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d() %>%
  layer_conv_2d(
    filters = 32, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
    padding = "same",
    activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d() %>%
  layer_conv_2d(
    filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
    padding = "same",
    activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d() %>%
  layer_flatten() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 300) %>%
  layer_dropout(.1) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "tanh")


# Compile and fit model
model %>%
  compile(
    optimizer = "sgd",
    loss = "mean_squared_error",
    metrics = "mean_squared_error")

model %>%
  fit_generator(
    gen(100, arqs_train),
    steps_per_epoch = 100,
    validation_data = gen(100, arqs_test),
    validation_steps = 10
  )

So? Can you get it 100% right? Or is it impossible?

Happy R’ing!

item.title: How to make R tell you on telegram that bitcoin is cheap
item.dc:creator: Athos Damiani
item.description:
The highlight of the story is R sending a message to Telegram. Just to get you motivated, I’ll tell you about something fun I did with telegram and bitcoin prices.

Hero of the day: Luca Biglia, author of the R telegram package.

What we’ll do

As I mentioned, I’ll build a bitcoin tracker to illustrate, and by the end of the post we’ll have made R send a telegram when the price of bitcoin hits a given level.

Ingredients

For today’s craft project we’ll need:

  • A telegram bot
  • The R package library(telegram)
  • The BlinkTrade API
  • String and a tube of glue

The steps we need to follow to get there are:

  1. Create an .Rproj (RStudio project).
  2. install and load the R telegram package.
  3. Create a telegram bot with the help of BotFather.
  4. Connect R to the bot.
  5. Query and store bitcoin prices every 30 seconds.
  6. create an infinite loop in R to track the prices nonstop.
  7. Make R send us a message when the price of bitcoin is above X, for example.
  8. (extra) Come up with wild ideas of what to do with telegram + R.

Introduction to the components

First of all, a brief introduction to the things that will show up here:

  • telegram: just like Whatsapp, but better.
  • BotFather: a contact on your phone (on telegram) that helps you create a telegram bot.
  • bitcoin: a successful digital currency.
  • BlinkTrade: among other things, provides an API for real-time bitcoin values.

Bitcoin tracker

Go ahead and create your .Rproj, run install.packages("telegram");library(telegram) and let’s go straight to the third step.

Step 3: Telegram bot - Create a bot

A bot is like one more person in your telegram contact list, except they are machines instead of humans and respond to specific commands. The fun part is that you can customize these commands any way you like! You just need a purpose and to know how to program it.

The README on the package’s github is very good! I’ll summarize what’s there with small changes:

  1. Go to your telegram and search for BotFather as if you were looking for a person in your contact list. Start a chat with him!
  2. Send the text “/start” and then “/newbot”. Give your bot a name (it can be a cute name) and then a username for your bot, which must end in bot.
  3. Now copy the token BotFather sent you and paste it into .Renviron. My bot has the username AthosDamianiBot, so I should name the variable like this:

If you use this naming convention you can use the bot_token() function to get your token. Otherwise you’ll have to resort to Sys.getenv().

NOTE: Restart R so that .Renviron takes effect.

Step 4: Telegram bot - Connect to R

  1. Load the package and create a TGBot object for the bot you created earlier:
library(telegram)

bot <- TGBot$new(token = bot_token('AthosDamianiBot'))

bot$getMe()

  1. Now we need the chat_id. To get it, search for your bot on telegram as if it were a contact (just like you did with BotFather) and start a chat with it.

  2. In R, call the bot$getUpdates() method to get the messages you sent it into R and, finally, find the chat_id hidden in msgs.

msgs <- bot$getUpdates()

msgs$message$chat$id[1]

[1] 135717340
  1. With the chat_id in hand, set it as the default chat_id.
bot$set_default_chat_id(135717340)

At this point we’re ready to interact with our bot!

Step 5: Query bitcoin prices

Bitcoin prices are provided by the BlinkTrade API, which is very simple to use: just grab the json that the url in the code below returns. While I’m at it, I give it a little polish to make it a data.frame with the query date attached.

library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)

safe_fromJSON <- safely(fromJSON, as.numeric(NA))
nova_consulta_list <- safe_fromJSON("https://api.blinktrade.com/api/v1/BRL/ticker?crypto_currency=BTC")

nova_consulta <- nova_consulta_list$result %>%
        as.tibble %>%
        mutate(timestamp = lubridate::now())

nova_consulta
# A tibble: 1 x 9
      high      vol      buy  last      low   pair  sell vol_brl           timestamp
     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <chr> <dbl>   <dbl>              <dttm>
1 14438.21 511.5911 14077.01 14200 13801.04 BTCBRL 14200 7257317 2017-08-18 17:09:44

NOTE: I used the safely() adverb because the API can choke at any moment, which would make R return an error that would stop the price tracking.

Step 6: Infinite loop to track the prices

The skeleton of the tracker is made of an infinite loop (while(TRUE)), a historico.RData data.frame, a wait time between one query and the next (30 seconds by default) and the query itself.

# initializes historico.RData
# historico <- nova_consulta
# save(historico, file = "historico.RData")

acompanhar_bitcoin <- function(frequencia = 30) {
  load("historico.RData")

  # infinite loop
  while(TRUE) {
    # gets the brazilian bitcoin quote (BTCBRL) from the blinktrade API
    nova_consulta_list <- safe_fromJSON("https://api.blinktrade.com/api/v1/BRL/ticker?crypto_currency=BTC")

    # checks whether the API returned a list
    if("list" %in% class(nova_consulta_list$result)) {
      nova_consulta <- nova_consulta_list$result %>%
        as.tibble %>%
        mutate(timestamp = lubridate::now())

      # ---------------------
      #
      # space reserved for the rules!
      #
      # ---------------------

      # stores the query
      historico <- bind_rows(historico, nova_consulta)
      save(historico, file = "historico.RData")
    }
  }
  Sys.sleep(frequencia)
}

Step 7: Rules for telegram messages

Now it’s time to decide what the bot should warn us about! I left two simple examples below using the bot$sendMessage() method, which, as the name suggests, makes the bot send us a message. Now, every time the price of bitcoin is below R$13,600 or above R$14,600 I’ll know right away!

# if the quote value meets some criterion, sends a message via telegram.
if(nova_consulta$buy < 13600 & nova_consulta$last > 13900) {
  bot$sendMessage('baixa!')
  bot$sendMessage(nova_consulta$buy)
}

# ...

if(nova_consulta$buy > 14600 & nova_consulta$last < 14500) {
  bot$sendMessage('alta!')
  bot$sendMessage(nova_consulta$buy)
}

Extra Step: Wild ideas of what to do with telegram + R

Creativity rules here. You can send plots, sounds, stickers and any kind of media. I made a ggplot to keep an eye on the trend, so I could ask my bot to show me the plot at any time.

# ... this goes inside the acompanhar_bitcoin() function
p <- ggplot(historico %>%
              gather(indicador, valor, high, low, buy, sell, last)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = timestamp, y = valor, colour = indicador))
print(p)

You can also program commands to pass to the Bot so it builds something for us, for example, you could create a command to buy or sell bitcoins in real time!

Julio once created a bot that was practically R itself: you sent code as a message and it returned R’s output! Later I’ll ask him to post something about it.

Anyway, there’s room to be clever here. All it takes is that brilliant shower idea.

Homework: - Send the “gemidão do zap” (a Brazilian prank audio) to 3 friends with a line of code.

cheers!

item.title: Logistic Regression in: the world’s smallest deep learning
item.dc:creator: Athos Damiani
item.description:
Goals

The purpose of this post is to:

  • learn how to fit a logistic regression with keras
  • learn how to do a PCA with keras
  • bring Deep Learning closer to what most data analysts already knew.
  • encourage everyone who came before deep learning to study it and get comfortable with what’s new around it.
  • show that many professionals in the machine learning field already knew a large part of what deep learning uses.
  • raise a discussion about some myths that are not constructive for the data analyst community.

Motivation

I read statisticians, computer scientists, data engineers and the like questioning the future of Machine Learning and whether everything we knew before about statistical modeling had become obsolete (like this question on Quora: Should I Quit Machine Learning?).

And in conversations with people close to me I noticed some excitement about the novelty and frustration with the “obsolescence” of what they had spent time studying before.

To make it worse, opportunists rode this wave to do malicious marketing aimed at devaluing and dividing the data analyst community. Something very similar to what happened with other buzzwords like data science, big data, Python versus R and machine learning itself. Before, there was the classic advertising that company X used MACHINE LEARNING instead of predictive models. Now things have evolved and they resort to the word Deep Learning.

What really matters:

  1. Deep Learning is big news and has put Artificial Intelligence in the spotlight.
  2. Whoever knew Machine Learning before will be able to apply 95% of their knowledge in Deep Learning applications (including bayesianism, bootstrap, inference, probability and the whole lot).
  3. Deep Learning has to be seen as one more tool in the data analyst’s toolbox, not a replacement.

And to address this question I decided to fit a logistic regression using deep learning so that everyone who has ever fit a logistic regression can say they have built a neural network too! I confess a slightly provocative motivation, but what fun would it be otherwise? =P

What we’ll do

  • Logistic regression for (with glm)
  • Deep Learning for (with keras)
  • Show that logistic regression is not the best for and that Deep Learning goes beyond the limitation of linear models (with glm)
  • Deep Learning for (with keras)

Let’s get to work.

Packages

library(keras)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)

Logistic regression versus Deep Learning

Time to fit models to the same data in two different ways: logistic regression with glm and deep learning with keras.

Simulated data

logit <- function(p) log(p) - log(1 - p)
logistic <- function(x) 1/(1 + exp(-x))

n <- 100000
set.seed(19880923)
df <- data_frame(x = runif(n, -2, 2.5)) %>%
  mutate(y_1 = rbinom(n, 1, prob = logistic(-1 + 2 * x)), # y_1
         y_2 = rbinom(n, 1, prob = logistic(-1 + 2 * tanh(-1 + 2 * x)))) # y_2

The code above created two response variables (targets). In mathematical notation, they are defined as follows:

Response y_1

Response y_2

is linear in the logit of y_1, so logistic regression will do well at finding the parameters and . However, is not linear in the logit of y_2, so logistic regression won’t be able to faithfully represent the generator of y_2.

NOTE 1: The form has parameters inside the tanh function, which means our hypothesis for is no longer linear in the parameters. That’s why linear models (as the name suggests) are no longer suitable. And non-linearity is one of the generalizations neural networks give us! (yes, this is very relevant)

NOTE 2: of course, in this very simple one-variable case we could inspect the data to find good transformations of so that the logistic fit would be as good as a neural network’s, but if we added many other variables things would get complicated!

In neural network notation, the formulas above look like this:

Response y_1

Response y_2

What was a link function in GLM became an activation function in neural networks (at the end I talk more about vocabulary that changed).

A look at the data

# skimr::skim(df) %>% skim_print %>% with(numeric)  %>% mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 2) %>% DT::datatable()

df %>%
  gather(y_id, y_val, y_1, y_2) %>%
  mutate(x_cat = cut_number(x, n = 70)) %>%
  group_by(x_cat, y_id) %>%
  summarise(p = mean(y_val),
            n = n()) %>%
  mutate(logit_p = logit(p)) %>%
  gather(transformacao, p, p, logit_p) %>%
  mutate(transformacao = transformacao %>% fct_inorder %>% fct_recode("logit(p)" = "logit_p")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_cat, y = p, colour = y_id)) +
  theme_minimal(20) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~forcats::fct_inorder(transformacao), nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "x", colour = "resposta") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank())
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'x_cat'. You can override using the
## `.groups` argument.

The plot on the right shows that x is proportional to the logit of the probabilities of y_1 (in red), as it should be since we built it that way. With y_2 (in blue), it still looks like a sigmoid even after the transformation.

Fitting the models

Logistic regression for (with glm)

# glm model 1 -------------------------------------------------------
modelo_glm_1 <- glm(y_1 ~ x, data = df, family = binomial)
# coefficients
coef(modelo_glm_1)

# (Intercept)           x
#   -1.018434    2.011647

# accuracy
conf_matrix_glm_1 <- table(modelo_glm_1$fitted.values > 0.5, df$y_1)
sum(diag(conf_matrix_glm_1))/sum(conf_matrix_glm_1)

# [1] 0.85061

The estimates came out very close to the true values and .

The accuracy was 85%.

Deep Learning for (with keras)

Let’s build our hypothesis for .

# keras model 1 --------------------------------------------------------
# input: 1 variable: x.
input_keras_1 <- layer_input(1, name = "modelo_keras_1")

# output: there are no hidden layers, only the logit link function directly.
output_keras_1 <- input_keras_1 %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, name = "camada_unica") %>%
  layer_activation("sigmoid", input_shape = 1, name = "link_logistic") # sigmoid in tensorflow is the logistic

# keras_model is what builds our hypothesis f(x) (from E[y] = f(x))
modelo_keras_1 <- keras_model(input_keras_1, output_keras_1)

#
summary(modelo_keras_1)
Model
_____________________________________________________________
Layer (type)                     Output Shape    Param #
=============================================================
modelo_keras_1 (InputLayer)      (None, 1)       0
_____________________________________________________________
camada_unica (Dense)             (None, 1)       2
_____________________________________________________________
link_logistic (Activation)       (None, 1)       0
=============================================================
Total params: 2
Trainable params: 2
Non-trainable params: 0
_____________________________________________________________

The hypothesis we built has 2 parameters. Looks right! and .

Now it’s the loss function’s turn.

Since our goal is to build a logistic regression, we’ll choose the binary_crossentropy loss function, which is a synonym for the logistic deviance, the more common term in the statistics world.

The 'accuracy' metric doesn’t go into the loss function optimizer; we use it to compare the models we create. Here we’ll compare against the glm model fitted above (but, for example, with rare events 'accuracy' won’t be very informative, so we could use 'auc', 'gini', etc.).

modelo_keras_1 %>% compile(
  loss = 'binary_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_sgd(lr = 0.4),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

modelo_keras_1_fit <- modelo_keras_1 %>% fit(
  x = df$x,
  y = df$y_1,
  epochs = 20,
  batch_size = 1000,
  verbose = 0
)
# coefficients
modelo_keras_1 %>% get_layer("camada_unica") %>% get_weights

# [[1]]
#          [,1]
# [1,] 2.000054
#
# [[2]]
# [1] -1.015561

# accuracy
loss_and_metrics_1 <- modelo_keras_1 %>% evaluate(df$x, df$y_1, batch = 100000, verbose = 0)
loss_and_metrics_1[[2]]

# [1] 0.85053

Identical results! It had to be so, because we built the same hypothesis and the same loss function as glm.

Logistic regression for (with glm)

To model we’ll step onto ground that linear models don’t tread. First I try to fit a curve using x and the transformation tanh(x). Let’s suppose I chose this predictor after a thorough and lengthy inspection of the data (I tried to simulate roughly what I would do in a modeling task where I’d have to build the features by hand).

# glm model 2 -------------------------------------------------------
modelo_glm_2 <- glm(y_2 ~ x + tanh(x), data = df, family = binomial)

# coefficients
coef(modelo_glm_2)

# (Intercept)           x     tanh(x)
#  -1.6698641   0.3043212   2.0936353

# accuracy
conf_matrix_glm_2 <- table(modelo_glm_2$fitted.values > 0.5, df$y_2)
sum(diag(conf_matrix_glm_2))/sum(conf_matrix_glm_2)

# [1] 0.82204

82% accuracy, not bad. But the hypothesis and parameters were different from the true data generator. Let’s use neural networks to solve the non-linearity problem.

Deep Learning for (with keras)

Hypothesis for .

# keras model 2 --------------------------------------------------------
input_keras_2 <- layer_input(1, name = "modelo_keras_2")

output_keras_2 <- input_keras_2 %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, name = "camada_um") %>%
  layer_activation("tanh", input_shape = 1, name = "tanh_de_dentro") %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, input_shape = 1, name = "camada_dois") %>%
  layer_activation("sigmoid", input_shape = 1, name = "link_logistic")

modelo_keras_2 <- keras_model(input_keras_2, output_keras_2)

summary(modelo_keras_2)
Model
_____________________________________________________________
Layer (type)                Output Shape           Param #
=============================================================
modelo_keras_2 (InputLayer) (None, 1)              0
_____________________________________________________________
camada_um (Dense)           (None, 1)              2
_____________________________________________________________
tanh_de_dentro (Activation) (None, 1)              0
_____________________________________________________________
camada_dois (Dense)         (None, 1)              2
_____________________________________________________________
link_logistic (Activation)  (None, 1)              0
=============================================================
Total params: 4.0
Trainable params: 4.0
Non-trainable params: 0.0
_____________________________________________________________

Four ‘trainable’ parameters, that’s it! Two parameters inside the tanh and the two parameters outside. We need keras to give us back -1, 2, -1 and 2, the way we generated the data.

Cost function

modelo_keras_2 %>% compile(
  loss = 'binary_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_sgd(lr = 0.1),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

modelo_keras_2_fit <- modelo_keras_2 %>% fit(
  x = df$x,
  y = df$y_2,
  epochs = 20,
  batch_size = 100,
  verbose = 0
)

# coefficients
modelo_keras_2 %>% get_layer("camada_um") %>% get_weights

# [[1]]
#          [,1]
# [1,] 2.012015
#
# [[2]]
# [1] -1.058052

modelo_keras_2 %>% get_layer("camada_dois") %>% get_weights

# [[1]]
#          [,1]
# [1,] 1.981977
#
# [[2]]
# [1] -1.006567

# accuracy
loss_and_metrics_2 <- modelo_keras_2 %>% evaluate(df$x, df$y_2, batch_size = 100000)
loss_and_metrics_2[[2]]

# [1] 0.82221

82% accuracy as well, but now the parameters are very close to the ones that generated the data! We just saw a set of parameters being found even with a non-linear relationship between them and the mean.

The accuracy of the two models ended up about the same, but the plot of the hypotheses found (below) shows that the glm curve is worse than the keras curve.

df %>%
  select(x, y_2) %>%
  mutate(x_cat = cut_number(x, n = 50)) %>%
  group_by(x_cat) %>%
  summarise(p = mean(y_2),
            x = mean(x),
            keras = logistic(-1.006567 + 1.981977 * tanh(-1.058052 + 2.012015 * x)),
            glm = logistic(-1.6698641 + 0.3043212*x + 2.0936353 * tanh(x)),
            n = n()) %>%
  mutate(logit_p = logit(p)) %>%
  gather(Modelo, estimativa, keras, glm) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_cat, y = p)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x_cat, y = estimativa, colour = Modelo, group = Modelo)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "x", colour = "resposta")

(Bonus) PCA with an autoencoder

In practice, PCA and autoencoders are used to reduce the dimensionality of the data. PCA is a particular case of an autoencoder with only one layer and linear activation functions. The post Construindo Autoencoders (in Portuguese) shows how to build one and I recommend reading it.

Summary: the autoencoder is an amazing technique that generalizes PCA.

Discussion

In my opinion, what happened is that a lot of old, well-established stuff had its name changed and was presented as new, and this ended up overshadowing the truly relevant contributions of research around neural networks and deep learning.

You can see that Deep Learning has generalized quite a lot, so I declare this post a success if what’s written above sparked curiosity to learn more about deep learning and add it to the work that was already being done. It’s more worthwhile to bring all statistics and machine learning practitioners together in this novelty than to divide ourselves.

I believe that, more than ever, theoretical foundations and interpretation will have their value boosted by the spread of deep learning. With the myth that deep learning is a panacea, and with how easy it has made building a predictive model, there’s a risk of being buried by black boxes made by people who neglect important aspects like interpretability, causality and generalization. Maybe bayesianism will emerge (once again) as the solution to qualitative problems in an increasingly obscure world, shedding light on the excesses of complex models and the benefits of simple ones.

Speaking of bayesianism (and inference in general), the results already obtained for linear models still apply to deep learning. And we also have the advantage that all the other tools used in deep learning that don’t affect the linearity of the parameters can be used, like convolutional, recurrent, max pooling, drop out, autoencoder and so many others.

To wrap up, in practice I suggest applying deep learning with Keras, an amazing package that uses tensorflow or theano behind the scenes. I believe you’ll see many posts about it here! (feel free to pester Dan Falbel, one of the partners of curso-r.com, who is involved in developing this R package =]).

Fun facts

N-th smallest deep learning

Above we saw the smallest and the second smallest Deep Learnings (which have nothing deep about them =P). But we can go as deep as we want! The neural network representation comes out easily:

The mathematical representation, on the other hand, gets weird:

Vocabulary

Deep learning jargon and terms were inherited from a context different from the predictive modeling studied in statistics, and so countless synonyms came up. Some of them are:

  • activation function = link function
  • Softmax = multinomial likelihood
  • sigmoid = S-shaped function (in tensorflow the default is the logistic)
  • weights = parameters/betas/coefficients
  • binary crossentropy = deviance of the binomial distribution (logistic regression)

That’s it, we have to stay curious, ask questions and talk to each other. Cheers!

item.title: WoE in R with tidywoe
item.dc:creator: Athos Damiani
item.description:
WoE (weight of evidence) is a tool widely used in logistic regression applications, mainly in credit scoring. Simply put, it turns categories into numbers that reflect the difference between them by how well they separate Y = 1 from Y = 0.

If you don’t know what it is yet or want to read more about it, here is a text I enjoyed reading:

  • Data Exploration with Weight of Evidence and Information Value in R

The author of this text is Kim Larsen, creator of the Information package, which is complete and full of sophisticated tools around WoE. However, in my day-to-day work every now and then I had to write my own routines to build the WoE versions of my variables, even with several complete packages available. The main reason was that they weren’t very practical and didn’t fit the tidyverse philosophy. So I ended up gathering these routines into a package called tidywoe and putting it out there. The idea is to help the analyst gain time, readability and reproducibility. Here is how to use it.

Installation

To install it, just run the code below.

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("athospd/tidywoe")

Data and packages for the examples

library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidywoe)

# install.packages("FactoMineR")
data(tea, package = "FactoMineR")
tea_mini <- tea %>% select(breakfast, how, where, price)

How to use

There are two functions that matter: - add_woe() - adds the woe’s to a data frame. - woe_dictionary() - creates a dictionary that maps the categories to their woe’s.

add_woe()

The add_woe() function adds the WoE versions of the variables to your data sample.

tea_mini %>% add_woe(breakfast)
breakfast how where price how_woe where_woe price_woe
breakfast tea bag chain store p_unknown -0.0377403 -0.0451204 -0.2564295
breakfast tea bag chain store p_variable -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.1872882
Not.breakfast tea bag chain store p_variable -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.1872882
Not.breakfast tea bag chain store p_variable -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.1872882

You can pick the variables you want by selecting them just like in dplyr::select().

tea_mini %>% add_woe(breakfast, where:price)

woe_dictionary()

The woe_dictionary() function is one of the two parts needed to make add_woe() work (the other part is the data). It builds the dictionary of categories and their respective woe’s.

tea_mini %>% woe_dictionary(breakfast)
variable explanatory n_tot n_breakfast n_Not.breakfast p_breakfast p_Not.breakfast woe
how tea bag 170 80 90 0.5555556 0.5769231 -0.0377403
how tea bag+unpackaged 94 50 44 0.3472222 0.2820513 0.2078761
how unpackaged 36 14 22 0.0972222 0.1410256 -0.3719424
where chain store 192 90 102 0.6250000 0.6538462 -0.0451204

Using a custom dictionary

Often we want to adjust some woe values by hand to fix the order of the effects of a given ordinal variable. That’s why add_woe() can take a dictionary passed by the user. This is done through the .woe_dictionary argument.

The easiest way to do this is to build an initial dictionary with woe_dictionary() and then change its values to get the adjustments you want. Example:

# Build an initial dictionary
tea_mini_woe_dic <- tea_mini %>% woe_dictionary(breakfast)

# Tweak the woes a little
tea_mini_woe_dic_arrumado <- tea_mini_woe_dic %>% mutate(woe = if_else(explanatory == "p_unknown", 0, woe))

# Pass this dictionary to add_woe()
tea_mini %>% add_woe(breakfast, .woe_dictionary = tea_mini_woe_dic_arrumado)
breakfast how where price how_woe where_woe price_woe
breakfast tea bag chain store p_unknown -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.0000000
breakfast tea bag chain store p_variable -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.1872882
Not.breakfast tea bag chain store p_variable -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.1872882
Not.breakfast tea bag chain store p_variable -0.0377403 -0.0451204 0.1872882

Exploration example

woe_dictionary() returns a tidy table, very convenient for further exploration. For example, the table is ready for ggplot.

tea_mini_woe_dic_arrumado %>%
  mutate(explanatory = explanatory %>% as.factor %>% fct_reorder(woe)) %>%
  filter(variable %in% c("price", "how")) %>%
  ggplot() +
    geom_bar(aes(x = explanatory, y = woe), stat = "identity") +
    facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))

Here is the package’s github for contributions. I still plan to add a lot of new stuff to the package.

Cheers
